name: Kenneth L. Gentry Jr.
tradition: Reformed Presbyterian minister and author
bio: Gentry is the leading contemporary scholarly advocate of postmillennialism joined to partial (orthodox) preterism. His doctoral work, published as Before Jerusalem Fell, argues at length that Revelation was written under Nero before AD 70, and he reads most of Revelation's judgments as fulfilled in the Jewish War. He Shall Have Dominion is his systematic defense of postmillennial optimism grounded in the covenants, the Great Commission and Christ's present reign. He has represented postmillennialism and preterism in several multi-view volumes and debated Thomas Ice in print, while also writing against full preterism, which he regards as outside creedal orthodoxy.
works: The Great Tribulation: Past or Future? (with Thomas Ice, 1999)

name: Greg L. Bahnsen
tradition: Orthodox Presbyterian; Van Tillian apologist and theonomist
bio: Bahnsen was a philosopher, apologist and Orthodox Presbyterian minister best known for presuppositional apologetics and for theonomy, the view that the moral and judicial laws of the Old Testament remain normative. He was a convinced postmillennialist who taught that the gospel, working through the church and the means of grace, will bring the great majority of the world to faith before Christ returns. His lectures on the subject were published posthumously as Victory in Jesus. With Kenneth Gentry he wrote House Divided, a sustained reply to dispensational critics of Reconstructionist postmillennialism.

name: Loraine Boettner
tradition: Presbyterian (Princeton-trained) lay theologian
bio: Boettner, trained under the Old Princeton theologians, wrote the mid-twentieth-century standard defense of postmillennialism at a time when the view had largely fallen out of favour. The Millennium surveys the three millennial positions and argues that the world will be Christianized through the ordinary preaching of the gospel, leading to a long era of righteousness and peace before Christ returns. He represented postmillennialism in Robert Clouse's The Meaning of the Millennium (1977). He is also known for The Reformed Doctrine of Predestination.
works: Postmillennialism, in The Meaning of the Millennium (1977)

name: B. B. Warfield
tradition: Old Princeton Presbyterian
bio: Benjamin Breckinridge Warfield was the leading Princeton theologian of his generation. His essay The Millennium and the Apocalypse reads Revelation 20:1-10 not as a future earthly era but as a picture of the blessedness of departed saints reigning with Christ in heaven during the present age, an exegesis many classify as amillennial or idealist. Yet his broader eschatology was strongly optimistic: he expected the gospel to win the world before the end, and he argued that the vast majority of humanity would finally be saved. He is therefore claimed by both postmillennialists and amillennialists, and his label is disputed.
works: Are They Few That Be Saved? (1918)

name: Iain H. Murray
tradition: Reformed evangelical; co-founder of the Banner of Truth Trust
bio: Murray is a British minister, biographer and historian, co-founder of the Banner of Truth Trust. The Puritan Hope traces the 'hope' of English and Scottish Puritans that the gospel would spread through the nations, that the Jewish people would be converted in large numbers (from Romans 11), and that this would bring a season of worldwide blessing. The book is widely credited with reviving interest in historic, revival-centred postmillennialism among Reformed evangelicals. His many biographies (Edwards, Lloyd-Jones, Spurgeon) often highlight this eschatology of hope.

name: Keith A. Mathison
tradition: Reformed; Ligonier Ministries and Reformation Bible College
bio: Mathison is a Reformed theologian associated with R. C. Sproul's Ligonier Ministries and Reformation Bible College. Postmillennialism: An Eschatology of Hope presents a modest, non-theonomic postmillennialism built from a survey of Old and New Testament texts on the growth of the messianic kingdom. He also edited When Shall These Things Be?, a collection of essays by Reformed scholars arguing that full ('hyper') preterism departs from biblical and creedal teaching on the resurrection and Second Coming. His Dispensationalism: Rightly Dividing the People of God? is a Reformed critique of dispensational theology.
works: Dispensationalism: Rightly Dividing the People of God? (1995)

name: Douglas Wilson
tradition: Reformed evangelical (Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches), Moscow, Idaho
bio: Wilson is a pastor, author and founder of a classical-Christian education movement who is one of the most visible popular advocates of postmillennialism. He argues that Christ is reigning now and that the Great Commission will succeed in discipling the nations, transforming culture over long ages, before Christ returns. He holds a partial preterist reading of the Olivet Discourse and much of Revelation. He represented postmillennialism at the 2009 Desiring God panel moderated by John Piper, alongside Sam Storms (amillennial) and Jim Hamilton (historic premillennial).
works: Heaven Misplaced: Christ's Kingdom on Earth (2008)
When the Man Comes Around: A Commentary on Revelation (2019)

name: Gary DeMar
tradition: Reformed evangelical; long-time president of American Vision
bio: DeMar is a popular writer and speaker who led American Vision for decades. Last Days Madness argues that the 'last days' language, the Olivet Discourse's 'this generation' (Matthew 24:34) and much of Revelation refer to the first-century end of the old covenant order in AD 70, and that modern 'prophecy watching' misreads Scripture. He debated Dave Hunt and Thomas Ice on Christian Reconstruction (1988, 1989) and Ice on preterism and futurism (2002, 2006), and has debated Michael Brown on Israel and the church. Critics such as Ice describe his view as replacement theology; DeMar rejects that label.
works: The Reduction of Christianity (with Peter Leithart, 1988)

name: Jonathan Edwards
tradition: New England Congregationalist (Reformed); theologian of the Great Awakening
bio: Edwards, the leading theologian of the First Great Awakening, combined a historicist reading of Revelation (with the papacy as Antichrist) with a fervent postmillennial expectation. In A History of the Work of Redemption he traced God's plan through history toward a coming 'glorious' age in which the gospel, through outpourings of the Spirit and revival, would fill the earth before Christ's return. His Humble Attempt urged united prayer for such revival. He became a key source for later evangelical missionary optimism.
works: A History of the Work of Redemption (sermons 1739; published 1774)

name: R. J. Rushdoony
tradition: Orthodox Presbyterian; founder of the Chalcedon Foundation and of Christian Reconstruction
bio: Rushdoony, the founder of the Christian Reconstruction movement, argued that God's law applies to every sphere of life and that the church's task is to bring all things under Christ's lordship. His postmillennialism, set out in Thy Kingdom Come (a study of Daniel and Revelation), expected the progressive triumph of Christ's kingdom in history through the gospel and obedience to God's law. His Institutes of Biblical Law (1973) is the movement's foundational text. Critics charge the movement with confusing church and state; proponents answer that it seeks change by regeneration and persuasion, not coercion.

name: Charles Hodge
tradition: Old Princeton Presbyterian
bio: Hodge taught at Princeton Theological Seminary for over fifty years and his three-volume Systematic Theology became a standard Reformed textbook. In its eschatology he defended the 'common church doctrine' that Christ returns once, after the gospel has spread through the world and Israel has been converted, followed by a general resurrection and judgment. He criticized premillennialism as inconsistent with the New Testament's teaching of one coming and one resurrection. He typifies nineteenth-century American Presbyterian postmillennialism.

name: R. C. Sproul
tradition: Reformed (PCA); founder of Ligonier Ministries
bio: Sproul, founder of Ligonier Ministries, was one of the best-known Reformed teachers of his era. The Last Days According to Jesus defends a partial preterist reading of the Olivet Discourse and of many New Testament time-texts, arguing that taking 'this generation' seriously answers skeptics who claim Jesus wrongly predicted the end. He carefully distinguished this from full preterism and affirmed a future bodily return and resurrection. He did not firmly commit to a millennial position in that book, though he expressed sympathy for postmillennialism.
works: The Last Days According to Jesus (1998)

name: N. T. Wright
tradition: Anglican; former Bishop of Durham; New Testament historian
bio: Wright is among the most influential New Testament scholars of his generation. In Jesus and the Victory of God he argues that Jesus' 'Son of Man coming on the clouds' language (Daniel 7) referred to his vindication and the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70 rather than to the end of the space-time universe, a reading close to partial preterism. In Surprised by Hope and The Resurrection of the Son of God he strongly affirms a future bodily resurrection and new creation, with the 'second coming' texts in Paul pointing to Christ's future appearing. He does not frame his views in millennial categories; his label here is approximate and disputed.
works: The Resurrection of the Son of God (2003)
Jesus and the Victory of God (1996)

name: Anthony A. Hoekema
tradition: Christian Reformed Church; Calvin Theological Seminary
bio: Hoekema taught systematic theology at Calvin Seminary. The Bible and the Future is a standard Reformed amillennial textbook, notable for emphasizing 'inaugurated eschatology' (the already/not yet) and the renewed earth as the final home of the redeemed. He preferred the term 'realized millennialism', reading Revelation 20 as the present reign of Christ and departed saints during the church age. He represented amillennialism in Clouse's The Meaning of the Millennium (1977).
works: Amillennialism, in The Meaning of the Millennium (1977)

name: Kim Riddlebarger
tradition: Reformed (United Reformed Churches); pastor in Anaheim and White Horse Inn co-host
bio: Riddlebarger, a former dispensationalist, wrote A Case for Amillennialism as an accessible defense of the view he calls the historic Protestant understanding of the millennial age. He stresses the 'two-age' structure of New Testament eschatology (this age and the age to come), Christ's present reign, and a single return bringing resurrection and judgment. The Man of Sin traces the development of the Antichrist doctrine. He blogs and teaches widely through his Riddleblog and White Horse Inn.
works: The Man of Sin: Uncovering the Truth about the Antichrist (2006)

name: Sam Storms
tradition: Reformed charismatic (Baptist); pastor and author
bio: Storms, a former dispensationalist, set out his mature view in Kingdom Come: The Amillennial Alternative, one of the most thorough recent defenses of amillennialism. He works through Daniel's seventy weeks, the Olivet Discourse, Romans 11, 2 Thessalonians 2 and Revelation 20, arguing for one return of Christ bringing a general resurrection and judgment. He admits sympathy for postmillennial optimism but judges it unable to account for the New Testament's emphasis on suffering through the whole age. He represented amillennialism at the 2009 Desiring God panel.

name: G. K. Beale
tradition: Reformed evangelical New Testament scholar
bio: Gregory K. Beale's massive commentary on Revelation in the NIGTC series is perhaps the most influential scholarly amillennial treatment of the book. He calls his approach a 'redemptive-historical form of modified idealism': Revelation's symbols portray the conflict between the church and evil throughout the whole age between Christ's comings, with a final consummation. He emphasizes Revelation's pervasive Old Testament allusions and argues for the later date (c. AD 95). His later work develops a New Testament biblical theology centred on new creation.
works: The Temple and the Church's Mission (2004)

name: Geerhardus Vos
tradition: Dutch-American Reformed; Princeton Theological Seminary
bio: Vos, often called the father of Reformed biblical theology, taught at Princeton from 1893 to 1932. The Pauline Eschatology argues that eschatology is not an appendix but the very framework of Paul's theology: in Christ's resurrection the 'age to come' has already broken into 'this age', while its fullness awaits his return. His two-age diagram became foundational for later amillennial and inaugurated-eschatology writers. He rejected chiliasm, reading the New Testament as teaching one return and one general resurrection.
works: Biblical Theology: Old and New Testaments (1948)

name: Augustine of Hippo
tradition: Latin Church Father; bishop of Hippo in North Africa
bio: Augustine's City of God, Book XX, gave the Western church its standard reading of Revelation 20. Having once held a form of chiliasm, he came to read the binding of Satan as Christ's present restraint of the devil so that the nations can be evangelized, the first resurrection as spiritual regeneration, and the thousand years as the present age of the church. Building on the Donatist exegete Tyconius, this reading shaped medieval and Reformation eschatology. Amillennialists regard him as their great forebear; some postmillennialists also claim aspects of his thought.
works: The City of God (413–426), esp. Book XX

name: William Hendriksen
tradition: Christian Reformed Church; New Testament commentator
bio: Hendriksen's More Than Conquerors popularized the 'progressive parallelism' approach to Revelation. He divided the book into seven parallel sections, each spanning the period from Christ's first coming to his second, with increasing intensity toward the end. On this reading Revelation 20 recapitulates the whole church age rather than following chapter 19 chronologically. The book has been a standard amillennial handbook for decades.
works: The Bible on the Life Hereafter (1959)
New Testament Commentary series (Matthew, Luke, Pauline epistles)

name: Samuel E. Waldron
tradition: Reformed Baptist (1689 Confession); pastor and seminary professor
bio: Waldron is a Reformed Baptist pastor-theologian known for his exposition of the 1689 Baptist Confession. The End Times Made Simple presents amillennialism through a simple framework: the return of Christ is one event, bringing one resurrection, one judgment and the end of the world. He also wrote a book-length reply to John MacArthur's claim that every self-respecting Calvinist should be a premillennialist. His approach stresses the analogy of Scripture, letting clearer New Testament texts interpret Revelation 20.
works: MacArthur's Millennial Manifesto: A Friendly Response (2008)
A Modern Exposition of the 1689 Baptist Confession of Faith (1989)

name: Dennis E. Johnson
tradition: Presbyterian (PCA); Westminster Seminary California
bio: Johnson is professor emeritus of practical theology at Westminster Seminary California. Triumph of the Lamb is a pastoral, redemptive-historical commentary that reads Revelation's visions as symbolic portrayals of the conflict between Christ and Satan spanning the church age, with a strong focus on the comfort they gave suffering churches. He interprets Revelation 20 within the recapitulation framework common to Reformed amillennialists. His work on Christ-centred preaching complements his eschatology.
works: Triumph of the Lamb: A Commentary on Revelation (2001)

name: George Eldon Ladd
tradition: Baptist; Fuller Theological Seminary
bio: Ladd was the most important twentieth-century advocate of historic (non-dispensational) premillennialism. He developed the 'already/not yet' understanding of the kingdom of God as God's dynamic reign, inaugurated in Jesus and consummated at his return. The Blessed Hope argued for a posttribulational rapture against dispensational pretribulationism, and his Revelation commentary combines a futurist reading of the consummation with a literal intermediate kingdom after Christ's return. He represented historic premillennialism in Clouse's The Meaning of the Millennium.
works: Jesus and the Kingdom (1964; rev. as The Presence of the Future, 1974)
A Commentary on the Revelation of John (1972)
A Theology of the New Testament (1974)

name: Craig L. Blomberg
tradition: Evangelical Baptist; Denver Seminary New Testament scholar
bio: Blomberg is a prolific New Testament scholar best known for work on the historical reliability of the Gospels. With Sung Wook Chung he edited A Case for Historic Premillennialism, which defends a premillennial reading of Revelation 20 without the dispensational distinction between Israel and the church and with a posttribulational return of Christ. He argues that the sequence of Revelation 19 to 20 and the two resurrections of Revelation 20:4-6 are most naturally read as a future earthly kingdom.
works: A Case for Historic Premillennialism (ed. with Sung Wook Chung, 2009)
The Historical Reliability of the Gospels (1987)

name: Douglas J. Moo
tradition: Evangelical; New Testament scholar (Trinity, Wheaton)
bio: Moo is a leading evangelical New Testament scholar known especially for commentaries on Romans. He has twice argued for the posttribulational rapture in multi-view volumes: in the 1984 Zondervan book with Feinberg and Archer, and in Hultberg's Three Views on the Rapture (2010). He contends that 1 Thessalonians 4, 2 Thessalonians 2 and the Olivet Discourse describe a single public coming of Christ after the tribulation. His Romans commentary also expects a future large-scale conversion of ethnic Israel (Romans 11:26).
works: The Epistle to the Romans (NICNT, 1996; 2nd ed. 2018)
The Case for the Posttribulation Rapture Position (1984)
A Case for the Posttribulation Rapture (2010)

name: Wayne Grudem
tradition: Evangelical, Reformed Baptist-leaning; Phoenix Seminary
bio: Grudem's Systematic Theology is one of the most widely used evangelical textbooks. In its eschatology chapters he describes all three millennial positions fairly before arguing for historic premillennialism with a posttribulational return, on the grounds that Revelation 20 follows chapter 19 sequentially and that two resurrections are distinguished. He stresses that Christ's return could be soon yet has preconditions such as the gospel's spread and the man of lawlessness. He urges charity among evangelicals on these questions.

name: Papias of Hierapolis
tradition: Early Church Father; bishop in Asia Minor
bio: Papias was an early second-century bishop who collected oral traditions from those who had heard the apostles and 'the elder John'. His work survives only in fragments quoted by Irenaeus and Eusebius. He taught a future earthly kingdom of a thousand years after the resurrection, describing its extraordinary fruitfulness. Eusebius later judged him 'of very limited understanding' for taking apostolic sayings too literally, a verdict premillennialists regard as biased by Eusebius's own anti-chiliasm.
works: Expositions of the Sayings of the Lord (fragments)

name: Justin Martyr
tradition: Early Church Father; apologist in Rome
bio: Justin, a philosopher converted to Christianity and later martyred in Rome, wrote the earliest extended defense of chiliasm outside Papias. In Dialogue with Trypho (chapters 80-81) he says that he and other fully orthodox Christians expect a resurrection of the flesh and a thousand years in a rebuilt Jerusalem, citing Isaiah 65 and Revelation 20. Importantly, he also acknowledges that many true Christians did not share this view. Premillennialists cite him as evidence of early chiliasm; others note his admission of diversity.

name: Irenaeus of Lyons
tradition: Early Church Father; bishop of Lyons; disciple of Polycarp
bio: Irenaeus, who knew Polycarp (a disciple of John), wrote Against Heresies to refute Gnosticism. In Book V he argues for a future earthly kingdom of the righteous after the resurrection, as the fitting reward of creation's renewal, and expects a personal Antichrist who will reign three and a half years. He also offers the earliest discussion of the number 666 and states that Revelation was seen near the end of Domitian's reign, a key witness for the late date (though its wording is debated by early-date advocates).

name: Charles C. Ryrie
tradition: Dispensational evangelical; Dallas Theological Seminary
bio: Ryrie was the most influential systematizer of classical (revised) dispensationalism in the mid-twentieth century. Dispensationalism Today (revised as Dispensationalism) named the 'sine qua non' of the system: a consistent distinction between Israel and the church, consistently literal (normal) hermeneutics, and the glory of God as the unifying purpose of history. The Ryrie Study Bible spread these views widely. He defended a pretribulational rapture and a future earthly millennium in which God's promises to national Israel are fulfilled.

name: John F. Walvoord
tradition: Dispensational evangelical; president of Dallas Theological Seminary
bio: Walvoord led Dallas Theological Seminary from 1952 to 1986 and was among the most prolific dispensational writers on prophecy. The Millennial Kingdom defended premillennialism against amillennialism and postmillennialism, and The Rapture Question argued for a pretribulational rapture. His commentaries on Daniel and Revelation read the prophetic portions futuristically, with Daniel's seventieth week as a future seven-year tribulation. He was a central figure in popularizing dispensational eschatology in American evangelicalism.
works: Daniel: The Key to Prophetic Revelation (1971)

name: J. Dwight Pentecost
tradition: Dispensational evangelical; Dallas Theological Seminary
bio: Pentecost taught at Dallas Seminary for decades. Things to Come is a comprehensive textbook of dispensational eschatology covering hermeneutics, the biblical covenants, the rapture, the tribulation, the millennium and the eternal state. It argues that the unconditional Abrahamic, Davidic and New covenants require a literal future fulfilment for national Israel. It remains a standard reference for classical dispensational prophecy.

name: Thomas Ice
tradition: Dispensational Baptist; co-founder of the Pre-Trib Research Center
bio: Ice co-founded the Pre-Trib Research Center with Tim LaHaye and has been its leading scholarly voice. A former theonomist, he became one of the most active critics of Reconstructionist postmillennialism and of preterism. He debated Gentry in The Great Tribulation: Past or Future? (1999), debated Gary North, Gary DeMar and Ken Gentry with Dave Hunt (1988, 1989), and debated DeMar on preterism at Biola (2002) and again in 2006. With Mark Hitchcock he answered Hank Hanegraaff's The Apocalypse Code.
works: Dominion Theology: Blessing or Curse? (with H. Wayne House, 1988)
The Great Tribulation: Past or Future? (with Kenneth Gentry, 1999)
The End Times Controversy (ed. with Tim LaHaye, 2003)
Breaking the Apocalypse Code (with Mark Hitchcock)

name: John Nelson Darby
tradition: Plymouth Brethren; former Church of Ireland clergyman
bio: Darby, a leader of the early Plymouth Brethren, is regarded as the founder of dispensationalism. From around the early 1830s he taught a sharp distinction between Israel (God's earthly people) and the church (his heavenly people), and a secret pretribulational rapture removing the church before the prophetic clock resumes with Daniel's seventieth week. His extensive travels in Britain, Europe and North America spread these views, which shaped the Bible conference movement and the Scofield Reference Bible. The precise origins of the pretribulational rapture idea remain debated.
works: The Collected Writings of J. N. Darby (34 vols)
Synopsis of the Books of the Bible

name: C. I. Scofield
tradition: Congregationalist pastor and Bible teacher
bio: Cyrus Ingerson Scofield edited the Scofield Reference Bible (Oxford University Press, 1909; revised 1917), whose notes set out seven dispensations, the Israel-church distinction, a pretribulational rapture and a future millennial kingdom. It became the most influential vehicle of dispensational theology in the English-speaking world for much of the twentieth century. His Rightly Dividing the Word of Truth summarized the system's hermeneutic.
works: Rightly Dividing the Word of Truth (1888)

name: Darrell L. Bock
tradition: Progressive dispensationalist; Dallas Theological Seminary
bio: Bock is a New Testament scholar and, with Craig Blaising, a principal architect of progressive dispensationalism. That view holds that the Davidic kingdom has been inaugurated through Christ's resurrection and enthronement (Acts 2) while its full, earthly and national fulfilment for Israel awaits the millennium. He edited Three Views on the Millennium and Beyond (1999) and represented progressive dispensationalism in Covenantal and Dispensational Theologies (2022).
works: Three Views on the Millennium and Beyond (ed., 1999)

name: Craig A. Blaising
tradition: Progressive dispensationalist; Southwestern Baptist Theological Seminary
bio: Blaising co-authored Progressive Dispensationalism with Darrell Bock and wrote the premillennial essay in Three Views on the Millennium and Beyond. He argues that a holistic, 'new creation' eschatology requires the renewal of nations, land and Israel, not only individual salvation. In Hultberg's Three Views on the Rapture he defended the pretribulational position by linking the rapture to the Day of the Lord coming as a thief. He has also traced the history of premillennialism in the early church.
works: Premillennialism, in Three Views on the Millennium and Beyond (1999)
A Case for the Pretribulation Rapture (2010)

name: Robert L. Saucy
tradition: Progressive dispensationalist; Talbot School of Theology
bio: Saucy taught theology at Talbot for over five decades. The Case for Progressive Dispensationalism argues for more continuity between Israel and the church than classical dispensationalism allowed, while maintaining a future for national Israel. He represented progressive dispensationalism in Perspectives on Israel and the Church: 4 Views (2015).

name: Michael J. Vlach
tradition: Dispensational; The Master's Seminary
bio: Vlach is a leading contemporary dispensational theologian and critic of supersessionism. Has the Church Replaced Israel? examines the historical and theological case for 'replacement' or 'fulfillment' theology and argues that the New Testament affirms a future restoration of national Israel. He represented the traditional dispensational reading of Romans 9-11 in Three Views on Israel and the Church. His later work presents a 'new creation' model of eschatology in which nations and Israel have tangible roles.
works: Dispensationalism: Essential Beliefs and Common Myths (2008)

name: Albert Barnes
tradition: New School Presbyterian; Philadelphia pastor
bio: Barnes was a widely read American Presbyterian commentator whose Notes covered the whole Bible. His Notes on Revelation follow the historicist scheme, reading the seals, trumpets and vials as successive events in church and world history, including the fall of Rome, the rise of Islam and the papacy. Like many nineteenth-century evangelicals he combined this with an optimistic expectation of the gospel's eventual worldwide triumph.
works: Notes on the Book of Revelation (1852)

name: Edward Bishop Elliott
tradition: Church of England (evangelical) clergyman
bio: Elliott's four-volume Horae Apocalypticae is the most elaborate historicist commentary on Revelation ever written. Using the day-year principle, he correlated each vision with events from the first century to his own day, identifying the papacy as the Beast and Antichrist. He was premillennial, expecting Christ's return before the millennium. His work was the standard reference for nineteenth-century British historicists.

name: Max R. King
tradition: Churches of Christ minister; later founder of 'transmillennialism'
bio: King, a Churches of Christ minister, developed what he called 'covenant eschatology', the main modern form of full preterism. The Spirit of Prophecy (1971) and The Cross and the Parousia (1987) argue that all biblical prophecy, including the Second Coming, resurrection and judgment, was fulfilled in the transition from the old covenant to the new, culminating in AD 70, with the 'resurrection' understood corporately. Critics, including Reformed and Churches of Christ writers, regard this as a denial of the creedal future bodily resurrection; proponents reply that the creeds must be tested by Scripture's time-statements.
works: The Cross and the Parousia of Christ (1987)

name: Don K. Preston
tradition: Covenant Eschatology; formerly Churches of Christ
bio: Preston is one of the most prolific living advocates of full preterism ('covenant eschatology'), author of many books and a frequent formal debater. He argues that the Old Testament promises of resurrection and kingdom belong to Israel and were fulfilled when the old covenant age ended in AD 70, so that the Second Coming and resurrection are past. His opponents have included Thomas Ice and Michael Brown, the latter in a debate on Romans 11. Critics regard full preterism as outside creedal orthodoxy because it denies a future bodily return and resurrection.
works: We Shall Meet Him in the Air (2010)

name: Steve Gregg
tradition: Non-denominational evangelical Bible teacher and radio host
bio: Gregg is a Bible teacher and host of The Narrow Path radio programme. Revelation: Four Views sets the preterist, historicist, futurist and spiritual (idealist) interpretations side by side in parallel columns verse by verse, without arguing for one, and has become a standard reference for comparing approaches. In his own teaching he leans toward a partial preterist reading of much of Revelation and an amillennial view of chapter 20.
works: All You Want to Know About Hell (2013)

name: Marvin Rosenthal
tradition: Baptist; Jewish-Christian ministry leader (Zion's Hope)
bio: Rosenthal, a former pretribulationist and director of the Friends of Israel ministry, popularized the 'pre-wrath' rapture position in The Pre-Wrath Rapture of the Church (1990), building on work by Robert Van Kampen. He argued that the church will face the Antichrist's persecution during the 'great tribulation' in the second half of Daniel's seventieth week but will be raptured before the Day of the Lord's wrath, signalled by the sixth seal's cosmic disturbances. He later founded Zion's Hope and the Holy Land Experience in Orlando.
works: The Pre-Wrath Rapture of the Church (1990)

name: Alan E. Kurschner
tradition: Evangelical; prewrath advocate (Eschatos Ministries)
bio: Kurschner is a leading contemporary teacher of the prewrath rapture view. Antichrist Before the Day of the Lord argues from the Olivet Discourse, 2 Thessalonians 2 and Revelation 6 that the church will see the Antichrist's revelation and persecution, with the rapture occurring when the great tribulation is cut short and the Day of the Lord's wrath begins. He writes from a futurist premillennial framework that does not depend on classical dispensationalism.
works: Antichrist Before the Day of the Lord (2013)

name: Robert H. Gundry
tradition: Evangelical; Westmont College New Testament scholar
bio: Gundry, a student of F. F. Bruce, taught New Testament at Westmont College. The Church and the Tribulation (1973) is one of the most rigorous exegetical cases for a posttribulational rapture, arguing that the church will pass through the tribulation and meet the Lord at his single, visible coming. First the Antichrist (1997) continued the argument against pretribulationism.
works: Matthew: A Commentary on His Literary and Theological Art (1982)

name: Gleason L. Archer Jr.
tradition: Evangelical Old Testament scholar; Trinity Evangelical Divinity School
bio: Archer was a distinguished Old Testament scholar and linguist. In the 1984 multi-view volume The Rapture: Pre-, Mid-, or Post-Tribulational? he argued for a midtribulational rapture, placing the church's removal at the midpoint of Daniel's seventieth week before the outpouring of divine wrath. He is also known for his Survey of Old Testament Introduction and Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties.
works: A Survey of Old Testament Introduction (1964)
The Case for the Mid-Seventieth-Week Rapture Position (1984)

name: Peter J. Gentry
tradition: Reformed Baptist; Southern Baptist Theological Seminary Old Testament scholar
bio: Peter Gentry is an Old Testament and Septuagint scholar who, with Stephen Wellum, wrote Kingdom through Covenant. Gentry contributed the exegetical analysis of the biblical covenants (Noahic, Abrahamic, Mosaic, Davidic and New), arguing that they progressively unfold God's kingdom and find their fulfilment in Christ. The resulting 'progressive covenantalism' stands between covenant theology and dispensationalism. He also wrote on Daniel's seventy weeks, reading them as fulfilled in Christ.
works: Kingdom through Covenant (with Stephen Wellum, 2012; 2nd ed. 2018)
God's Kingdom through God's Covenants (with Wellum, 2015)

name: Stephen J. Wellum
tradition: Reformed Baptist; Southern Baptist Theological Seminary systematic theologian
bio: Wellum co-authored Kingdom through Covenant and is the principal theological voice of progressive covenantalism. He argues that the covenants must be read along the Bible's own storyline, with typology escalating to fulfilment in Christ, so that Israel's land and nationhood find their telos in Christ and the new creation. Against covenant theology he denies a single 'covenant of grace' administered through the Mosaic covenant; against dispensationalism he denies a separate future programme for national Israel. He represented the view in Covenantal and Dispensational Theologies (2022).

name: Craig S. Keener
tradition: Charismatic evangelical; Asbury Theological Seminary New Testament scholar
bio: Keener is a prolific New Testament scholar specializing in the cultural background of the New Testament. His Revelation commentary takes an eclectic approach, recognizing first-century referents while applying the visions to the whole church age and the end. With Michael Brown he co-wrote Not Afraid of the Antichrist (2019), arguing that believers should expect to endure tribulation and that Christ's return is a single posttribulational event.
works: The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament (1993)
Not Afraid of the Antichrist (with Michael Brown, 2019)

name: Richard Bauckham
tradition: Anglican; New Testament scholar (St Andrews, Cambridge)
bio: Bauckham is a leading British New Testament scholar. The Theology of the Book of Revelation and The Climax of Prophecy read Revelation as a Christian prophetic-apocalyptic critique of Roman imperial power, with a vision of the conversion of the nations through the church's faithful witness. He does not fit neatly into the four classic interpretive schools; he treats Revelation's first-century setting seriously while affirming a future consummation. He has also written on Jude, 2 Peter and the delay of the parousia.
works: The Theology of the Book of Revelation (1993)

name: John Owen
tradition: English Puritan (Congregationalist)
bio: Owen was the most eminent Puritan theologian. His sermons and writings express the Puritan hope of a future spread of the gospel, the conversion of the Jews and the downfall of Antichrist (identified with the papacy) before Christ's return, placing him in the postmillennial stream traced by Iain Murray. In a 1649 sermon he read the 'heavens and earth' to be shaken (Hebrews 12; 2 Peter 3) as including the old Jewish church-state, a reading partial preterists frequently cite. His massive Hebrews commentary develops his covenant theology.
works: The Shaking and Translating of Heaven and Earth (1649)
Exposition of the Epistle to the Hebrews (1668–84)

name: Martin Luther
tradition: Lutheran Reformer
bio: Luther at first doubted Revelation's value but in his 1530 preface read it as a prophecy of church history, identifying the papacy with Antichrist and the Turks with Gog and Magog. He expected the end to be near and rejected chiliasm; the Augsburg Confession (Article 17) condemns 'Jewish opinions' of a pre-resurrection earthly kingdom of the saints. His historicist identification of the papal Antichrist became standard in Protestant confessions and commentary for centuries.
works: Preface to the Revelation of St. John (1522, 1530)
On the Babylonian Captivity of the Church (1520)

name: John Calvin
tradition: Reformed Reformer (Geneva)
bio: Calvin wrote commentaries on almost every book of the Bible except Revelation. In the Institutes (III.25.5) he dismissed the chiliasts' thousand-year limit on the saints' reign as a 'fiction' too childish to need refutation, arguing that the thousand years of Revelation 20 does not describe the eternal blessedness of the church. He identified the papacy with the Antichrist of 2 Thessalonians 2. Amillennialists claim him as a forebear; postmillennialists point to his optimism about the kingdom's spread in his commentaries on the Psalms and prophets.
works: Commentaries on Daniel and the Psalms

name: Isaac Newton
tradition: English natural philosopher; heterodox Protestant (anti-Trinitarian)
bio: Newton devoted enormous effort to the interpretation of Daniel and Revelation, published posthumously as Observations upon the Prophecies of Daniel and the Apocalypse of St. John. He read the prophecies by the historicist method, applying the day-year principle and identifying the little horn with the papacy. Private papers reveal speculations that the end would not come before about 2060, which he offered to discourage date-setting rather than to fix a date. His non-Trinitarian views were not public in his lifetime.
works: Observations upon the Prophecies of Daniel and the Apocalypse of St. John (1733)

name: Origen of Alexandria
tradition: Greek Church Father; Alexandrian theologian
bio: Origen was the most important early proponent of allegorical and spiritual interpretation. In On First Principles (II.11) he criticized those who expect a material kingdom of eating, drinking and rebuilt Jerusalem, arguing that the promises refer to spiritual realities. His approach strongly influenced the decline of chiliasm in the Greek East and anticipates the idealist approach to Revelation. Some of his speculative views (such as the restoration of all things) were later condemned.

name: Eusebius of Caesarea
tradition: Greek Church Father; bishop and church historian
bio: Eusebius, the 'father of church history', preserves much of our knowledge of early eschatological debate. His Ecclesiastical History quotes Papias and reports the debate over Revelation's authorship, including Dionysius of Alexandria's doubts, and records Irenaeus's statement dating Revelation to Domitian's reign. He was hostile to chiliasm and saw Constantine's Christian empire as a fulfilment of God's purposes, an outlook sometimes called an early 'realized' or imperial eschatology.

name: Tertullian
tradition: Latin Church Father (Carthage); later associated with Montanism
bio: Tertullian, the first major Latin theologian, affirmed in Against Marcion (III.24) a thousand-year kingdom on earth after the resurrection in a divinely built Jerusalem, distinct from the heavenly kingdom that follows. He also wrote on the resurrection of the flesh against those who spiritualized it. His later sympathy for the Montanist movement, with its intense expectation of the New Jerusalem, made chiliasm suspect for some later writers.
works: On the Resurrection of the Flesh

name: James M. Hamilton Jr.
tradition: Southern Baptist; Southern Baptist Theological Seminary biblical theologian
bio: Hamilton is a biblical theologian whose work centres on God's glory in salvation through judgment. He defended historic premillennialism at the 2009 Desiring God panel and in his preaching commentary on Revelation. With Fred Zaspel he argued in Three Views on Israel and the Church for a future mass conversion of ethnic Israel without a separate role for Israel apart from the church.
works: God's Glory in Salvation through Judgment (2010)
Revelation: The Spirit Speaks to the Churches (2012)

name: Francisco Ribera
tradition: Spanish Jesuit
bio: Ribera's commentary on Revelation (c. 1590) placed most of the book (after the opening chapters) in the future, immediately before Christ's return, with a personal Antichrist reigning three and a half years. Protestant historians often describe this as a Counter-Reformation reply to the Protestant identification of the papacy with Antichrist. Modern futurists generally acknowledge him as an early systematic futurist while noting that futurist elements go back to Irenaeus and Hippolytus.

name: Luis de Alcázar
tradition: Spanish Jesuit
bio: Alcázar's Vestigatio Arcani Sensus in Apocalypsi (1614) is usually cited as the first systematic preterist commentary on Revelation. He read the early chapters as the church's victory over Judaism (the fall of Jerusalem) and the later chapters as its victory over pagan Rome. Protestant historians often describe his work, like Ribera's, as a Counter-Reformation alternative to the historicist papal-Antichrist reading; preterists note that preterist readings of individual texts are much older.

name: William Milligan
tradition: Church of Scotland; University of Aberdeen
bio: Milligan was a Scottish Presbyterian scholar whose lectures and Expositor's Bible volume on Revelation are classic statements of the idealist (spiritual) approach. He argued that Revelation is not a calendar of events but a symbolic portrayal of principles governing the conflict between Christ and evil throughout the church age. His approach influenced later amillennial commentators.

name: Tyconius
tradition: North African Donatist lay theologian
bio: Tyconius wrote the Book of Rules, the first Latin handbook of biblical interpretation, and a now-lost commentary on Revelation. He read the Apocalypse spiritually as a description of the church throughout the present age, including the present binding of Satan and the 'first resurrection' as spiritual renewal. Augustine adopted and transmitted many of his ideas, making Tyconius a key source for later amillennial and idealist interpretation.

name: Lactantius
tradition: Latin Christian apologist; tutor to Constantine's son
bio: Lactantius's Divine Institutes, Book VII, contains one of the fullest early Christian accounts of the end: the world lasting six thousand years, a final tyrant, the return of Christ, and a seventh millennium of earthly peace and abundance before the final judgment. He represents the strong chiliastic tradition in the Latin West before Tyconius and Augustine reshaped it.
works: On the Deaths of the Persecutors

name: David Chilton
tradition: Reformed; Christian Reconstruction movement
bio: Chilton was a Reconstructionist pastor whose Paradise Restored offered a popular biblical theology of dominion and The Days of Vengeance a full preterist-postmillennial commentary on Revelation as a covenant lawsuit against apostate Jerusalem. Late in life he adopted full preterism, though he did not publish a full defense of it; his earlier works remain widely used by partial preterists.

name: J. Marcellus Kik
tradition: Presbyterian pastor and editor
bio: Kik's An Eschatology of Victory (published posthumously in 1971) combined a preterist exposition of Matthew 24 with a postmillennial reading of Revelation 20. He argued that the dividing line in Matthew 24 falls at verse 35 (or 36), with everything before it fulfilled in AD 70. His work influenced later writers such as Gentry and DeMar.

name: John MacArthur
tradition: Non-denominational Reformed-leaning evangelical; Grace Community Church and The Master's Seminary
bio: MacArthur pastored Grace Community Church in Sun Valley, California, for over five decades and led The Master's Seminary. His 2007 Shepherds' Conference address argued that consistent Calvinists should be premillennialists, since God's sovereign, unconditional election of Israel guarantees his promises to the nation. He held a pretribulational rapture and future millennium, while distancing himself from some traditional dispensational distinctives. Sam Waldron and others published replies.
works: Christ's Prophetic Plans (ed. with Richard Mayhue, 2012)

name: Tim LaHaye
tradition: Baptist pastor; co-founder of the Pre-Trib Research Center
bio: LaHaye was a pastor and author who, with Jerry B. Jenkins, wrote the Left Behind novels, which brought a pretribulational dispensational scenario to tens of millions of readers. He co-founded the Pre-Trib Research Center with Thomas Ice to defend futurism scholarly and co-edited The End Times Controversy against preterism. Critics such as Hank Hanegraaff targeted his approach as sensationalist; supporters credit him with renewing interest in prophecy and evangelism.
works: Left Behind series (with Jerry B. Jenkins, 1995–2007)
The End Times Controversy (ed. with Thomas Ice, 2003)

name: Mark Hitchcock
tradition: Dispensational Bible church pastor; Dallas Theological Seminary
bio: Hitchcock is a pastor and popular dispensational writer on prophecy who wrote his doctoral dissertation defending the late (Domitianic) date of Revelation against preterist arguments. With Thomas Ice he wrote Breaking the Apocalypse Code in reply to Hank Hanegraaff. His many popular books argue for a pretribulational rapture and a future seven-year tribulation.
works: Breaking the Apocalypse Code (with Thomas Ice)
The End: A Complete Overview of Bible Prophecy and the End of Days (2012)

name: Hal Lindsey
tradition: Dispensational evangelical; Dallas Theological Seminary graduate
bio: Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (1970) became one of the best-selling non-fiction books of its decade by connecting dispensational prophecy to the Cold War, the 1948 founding of Israel and Middle East politics. It popularized the expectation that the generation that saw Israel's rebirth would see Christ's return. Scholarly dispensationalists have often distanced themselves from his date-oriented speculations; critics cite them as a cautionary example of 'newspaper exegesis'.

name: Hank Hanegraaff
tradition: Evangelical apologist ('Bible Answer Man'); Eastern Orthodox since 2017
bio: Hanegraaff, longtime president of the Christian Research Institute, wrote The Apocalypse Code (2007), proposing an 'exegetical eschatology' that reads Revelation largely as fulfilled in the judgment on Jerusalem while affirming a future bodily return and resurrection. He sharply criticized the Left Behind scenario and Christian Zionism. Thomas Ice and Mark Hitchcock answered him in Breaking the Apocalypse Code. He joined the Eastern Orthodox Church in 2017.

name: Michael L. Brown
tradition: Messianic Jewish, charismatic evangelical; host of The Line of Fire
bio: Brown is a Messianic Jewish scholar of Semitic languages and a radio host and debater. He holds a historic (non-dispensational) premillennial, posttribulational view, set out with Craig Keener in Not Afraid of the Antichrist. He strongly affirms a future for ethnic Israel and has debated Gary DeMar on 'replacement theology' and full preterists Don Preston and Michael Sullivan.
works: Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus (5 vols, 2000–2010)
Not Afraid of the Antichrist (with Craig Keener, 2019)

name: J. Stuart Russell
tradition: English Congregationalist minister
bio: Russell's The Parousia (1878) is the classic Victorian argument that every New Testament prediction of Christ's coming was fulfilled within the generation ending in AD 70. He worked systematically through the time-statements of the Gospels, Epistles and Revelation. The book is foundational for modern full preterism and is also widely read by partial preterists, who accept its time-text arguments but reject its conclusions about the resurrection and final judgment.
